About $6,748 of the $7,000 converted, roughly 96%, is taxable income for 2025. That's because Luka's rollover IRA was still holding pre-tax money at year end.

**Why**

- On 10 Feb 2025 Luka put $7,000 into the new traditional IRA (SYN-12040003), nondeductible as planned. On 13 Feb he converted the $7,000 to his Roth (SYN-12040004).
- The pro-rata rule on Form 8606 doesn't look only at the account the money was converted from. It treats all of Luka's traditional IRAs as one pool, valued on 31 Dec 2025. His rollover IRA (SYN-12040002) was worth $187,544.92 that day, all of it pre-tax. The December 2024 plan to leave that account alone is what makes most of the conversion taxable.
- Only $7,000 / $194,544.92 = 3.598% of the converted money counts as tax-free basis. That's $251.87. The other $6,748.13 is taxable.
- The $6,748.13 of basis that wasn't used carries forward to 2026, so it isn't lost.
- The 1099-R shows $7,000 with "taxable amount not determined." Neither $7,000 nor $0 is the right figure to report.
- The 2025 result can't be undone, because a conversion can't be reversed (recharacterized).
